title: Archuleta County Wells: Depth, Yield and Cost
meta_description: Archuleta County wells have a 150 ft median depth and 10 gpm median yield. Review local records, drilling costs, water levels and buyer checks.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Archuleta County
intro_html:
A well budget in Archuleta County starts with the ground beneath the lot, not the county average. Recorded depths have a median of 150 ft, but the middle half runs from 65-260 ft. That spread matters when you are pricing land, arranging construction or comparing drilling bids.

Colorado DWR records contain 3,769 permitted wells countywide, with 2,230 recorded as constructed. These records provide a starting point for properties around Pagosa Springs and Arboles, but a permit alone does not establish that a working well exists.

sections.heading: Why a 150 ft Well Is Only a Starting Point
sections.html:
Among the 2,295 wells reporting depth, the median is 150 ft and the middle half falls between 65-260 ft. For a drilling bid, that means allowing for substantial footage variation rather than treating the median as a fixed stopping depth. The 90th-percentile depth is 450 ft.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer; Mancos and Dakota also appear. In fractured rock, usable water depends on the openings the borehole intersects, not just how far down the driller goes. Compare nearby completed wells around your actual parcel in Pagosa Springs or Arboles, especially those with similar terrain and aquifer descriptions.

sections.heading: Reported Output Usually Falls Around Household Needs
sections.html:
The 907 wells with reported pump yields have a median of 10.0 gpm, with a middle half of 5.0-15.0 gpm. That is encouraging for household planning, but a recorded drilling-time yield is not a guarantee of sustained production today. Ask for a current pumping and recovery test on an existing well.

Yield reports put 3% below 1 gpm. That is a small share, but a serious concern for a buyer: slow recovery may require storage, demand management or further investigation before closing. Domestic/household use accounts for 75% of permits. Actual permitted uses still control; available water does not automatically authorize irrigation or livestock watering.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Countywide Drop
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to resting water in the well, not the total drilled depth. Archuleta County's median is 42 ft below ground, and the middle half spans 10-100 ft. A relatively shallow resting level does not mean the well can be drilled that shallow; the borehole must reach a productive water-bearing zone.

The median measured level was 44 ft in the 2010s and 41 ft in the 2020s. Those figures do not suggest a dropping water table. However, only 163 records report static levels, and these are not necessarily repeat measurements from the same wells. They cannot establish a trend for your parcel.

sections.heading: Archuleta's Permit History and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
Permit issuance was highest in the listed decades during the 1990s, with 744 permits, followed by 671 in the 2000s. The records show 219 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. That partial decade should not be compared directly with a completed decade to judge demand.

The most active drillers in the records are Beeman Bros Drilling Inc (Beeman, J. L.) with 469, Justice Water Systems, Inc (Hellwege, Joel S.) with 288, and Smith Water Well Service (Sanders, O L) with 236. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Ask prospective drillers about recent work near your lot and the conditions they encountered.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Hole in Mountain Ground
sections.html:
The supplied cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, such as granite or gneiss, at $65-$100 per foot. At the county's 150 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $9,800-$15,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $15,800-$27,000.

Treat those figures as planning allowances, not a parcel-specific quote. The model does not establish your lot's geology. Ask the driller to identify casing and grout allowances, access requirements, and how extra footage is charged. Have the pump and trenching scope spelled out separately so a low drilling price is not mistaken for a complete working water system.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality, Well Failure and Septic Fit
sections.html:
The environmental mapping includes 12 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 10 historic mine features within about 10 miles. A mapped sampling site does not prove that a nearby domestic well is contaminated. Conversely, the absence of mapped EPA Superfund/cleanup sites does not establish that the water is safe. Use the locations to guide questions and laboratory testing.

Inspect casing, the wellhead and surface drainage, and confirm that proposed septic facilities can meet required separation rules. Low-yield records show why production testing matters; fractured bedrock also leaves the possibility of an unsuccessful borehole. Ask how the drilling contract handles that outcome before authorizing work.

sections.heading: Before Buying a Lot Near Pagosa Springs or Arboles
sections.html:
Start with the permit and completion report for the property, then compare neighboring wells for depth, yield and aquifer. Countywide statistics are useful context, but they should not override evidence from the same hillside or drainage. Records from nearby La Plata County or Mineral County are not substitutes for local comparisons.

Confirm permitted uses with DWR before relying on water for anything beyond the stated authorization. For a new build, coordinate the well location with drilling access, the driveway, house, septic layout and utility trench. Make an existing-well purchase contingent on acceptable production and water-quality results, and keep a contingency for work the records cannot predict.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Archuleta County?
faq.a: The median reported well depth is 150 ft, and the middle half ranges from 65-260 ft. The 90th-percentile depth is 450 ft. Fractured-bedrock conditions mean neighboring properties can require different depths, so use nearby completion reports to set a budget rather than assuming your well will stop at the county median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Archuleta County?
faq.a: The mountain-bedrock cost model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 150 ft median depth, drilling alone is about $9,800-$15,000; a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $15,800-$27,000. Request a site-specific bid that identifies access, casing, grout and extra-footage charges.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Archuleta County?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 10.0 gpm, with the middle half at 5.0-15.0 gpm. Among wells reporting yield, 3% are below 1 gpm. A historical yield entry does not prove present capacity. Before buying, arrange a pumping and recovery test and assess whether storage is needed for household demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Archuleta County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established at the individual well. Mapping identifies 12 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 10 historic mine features within about 10 miles, but proximity alone does not establish contamination. Obtain laboratory testing, inspect the wellhead and casing, and use nearby environmental records to decide whether additional contaminant testing is appropriate.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Archuleta County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a drop: static water levels were 44 ft below ground in the 2010s and 41 ft in the 2020s. Only 163 records report static levels, and the measurements may represent different wells. These figures cannot establish long-term conditions at a particular property.
